title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of workers' daily life on film
dek: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English class. When the giant factory finally disappeared, almost no one else had kept this archive.
why: Not industry analysis: a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The back half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and content people interested in the shift in manufacturing, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the Pearl River Delta factory era disappeared.
skip: The show promo and event notices at the start, 0:00-1:08, can be skipped.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value not matter
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process to make manufacturing more stable and the people more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean: anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. The machines had not yet replaced them, but a person's value already barely mattered. This was the underlying motive for his later picking up a camera and aiming it at his co-workers: inside a system built to erase individual difference, to record specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train felt like riding into a bandit's den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The car was already full at the Wuchang origin station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed a window with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. More than thirty hours without sitting, without drinking water; after getting off, his belly was badly swollen. At Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold like a piglet’ — first they took twenty-odd yuan and said it was for Dongguan, then on the expressway they demanded another ten for the toll, and if you refused someone came up and slapped you, and in the end you were dumped in the middle of nowhere to change vehicles. He says he used the phrase for years before he understood what it meant last year.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 jobs were hard to find, and men far harder than women: factory notices said outright they only hired women aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring sign by National Highway 107, and the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 some were dropping, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he was. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. Then he was told to spar; the other man did a split, he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: gate security at a hotel, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he agonised for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and she said if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was still 48 each, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — a huge drain on him in that era. At first he shot factory events, visiting guests, employee tug-of-war, assuming that photography was just a technical problem of getting things sharp. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he found there was so much learning in photography and he had no standard to measure by, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson is the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: The model-contest photos passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete them
points.body: In 2007 the factory started holding a model contest: workers in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms on stage, plus pole dancing. In 2008 he changed position, went behind the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience behind — and sent the files to Tencent in time; they went up on the portal and drew tens of millions of clicks in a morning. But online comments said this was picking a mistress for the boss and a lover for the plant manager; the framing was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure, and he was told to delete them. Tencent said they could only hide them, other sites' viral reposting could not be stopped, and in the end he was served a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: The photo of the woman worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
points.body: On 5 January 2011, as a senior supervisor, he went into the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. Clean-room work allowed four minutes' rest after two hours; the changing area was hung with unused clean-room suits, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He took one or two frames, and the man heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the advice he was given when learning photography was that ‘a photo where the subject looks at the lens is not a good photo’, so he long avoided using it. Later Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organised the Off-Pix award; he submitted it and it was unexpectedly made the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterwards, he conceded it has its own pull — different viewers will have different inner responses, so a photographer should interpret his own photos as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed
points.body: Looking for work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. Factories' records were separate then, with no networked computer system, and social security did not have to be paid, so that set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system would not accept it — same ID number, same name, same household registration address — and the employer decided you were dishonest and zeroed your years of service. He says this will not do: our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those years of service are real. When even present-day life is insecure, it is impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years away.

points.h: Density: he shot for 20 years before seeing it everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he built a photo series around the density of migrant working life, which won an excellence award and the Alpa prize at the third Yingjishi Image Awards. A high-angle shot of a workers' assembly, heads packed with almost no gaps; a collective dormitory hung with clothes, from a distance airtight; workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers for bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual density. He says at first it was unconscious: shooting every day on his phone, shooting security training, shooting any co-worker he happened to see on the road, accumulating day by day, on and off for nearly 20 years. When there were so many eras in so many factories, he had not observed in that way; then one morning he found it so frightening that even a switch looked spectacular.

points.h: Time as warp, space as weft: a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The full thread he worked out: time as the warp, space as the weft, the life cycle as the guiding principle, capital's impact on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a composite three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text and objects. Later he changed method: starting from the keyword dagong (working for wages), he looked up ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related terms on Baidu, got 322, went into Baidu Images and screenshotted them all — this is the internet's understanding of dagong, to be shown together with his own photographed understanding in one huge exhibition space. He says this is us watching the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored. He compares himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers are carried by Sherpas, so I will just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets; later it meant being cheated en route to work by brokers and drivers who added charges layer by layer.
The researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
Magnum, the internationally known photography agency; Zhan Youbing once studied the work of its photographers on its website one by one.
A photography award organised by Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China; Zhan Youbing submitted to it and was shown as the lead image.

quotes.text: Back then, going out to work — it wasn't like you got on a bus. You felt like you'd got into a bandit's den.
This is the era: we watch the era from inside an illusory era, while the real era is ignored.
I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we reach will certainly not be poor; but if we can only see society in a single day, it will certainly be shallow.
